newsitem.title: USA: U.S Jan retail sales, Dec revision below forecasts.
newsitem.headline: U.S Jan retail sales, Dec revision below forecasts.

text.p: U.S. retail sales data for January and a downward revision in December sales figures indicate the first quarter is getting off to a slightly slower start than had been forecast, some economists said.

The government reported retail sales rose 0.6 percent in January and 0.4 percent when auto transactions were excluded. That was slightly weaker than the consensus forecast culled in a Reuters poll for 0.7 percent overall sales growth and a 0.6 percent increase when auto sales were set aside.
Also noteworthy, economists said, was a downward revision in December retail sales data.
December sales were first reported as being up 0.6 percent overall and up 0.6 percent excluding auto sales.
But the December figures were revised on Thursday to show a very modest 0.3 percent retail sales gain in total and no increase at all when auto sales were excluded.

The combination of the moderate sales gains in January and the subdued picture in December "gives the impression that things are softening up as we move into the first quarter," said Anthony Chan, chief economist at Banc One Investment Advisors Corp. "The report throws a little bit of cold water on the notion that we're starting off the new year with a lot of momentum," Chan said.

"The report was a touch weaker than expected, given the revisions to the prior month," said Christopher Low, senior economist, HSBC Markets Inc. "These are very friendly numbers for the (U.S. Treasury) market."
U.S. Treasury prices were mostly flat before the morning data releases -- a drop in weekly jobless claims was also reported -- but edged a bit higher afterwards.

The retail sales data gave the market "a bit of a boost," but the drop in new jobless claims to 309,000 from a revised 324,000 in the prior week countered some of that positive reaction, said analysts at MMS International Inc.
The 309,000 figure was the lowest level of new jobless claims since the week of July 27, the Labor Department said.

The claims drop underlined concerns about a tight labor market's potential for breeding inflation pressures, clouding the meaning of Thursday's economic data and leading to some divergent interpretations.

"My impression of the two numbers (jobless claims and retail sales data) is that the first quarter is starting off a little bit stronger than I thought," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp.
Michael Niemira, economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, concurred.
"When you step back, it says the consumer is alive and well and continues to spend," he said.
